A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GTPO research work. Their complete main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably despite additions and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical-reasoning evaluations, component ablations, training curves, and generated-code case studies in Section 5 and the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, another model family, non-math evaluations, embedding correlations, and tool-execution analyses.

M1.justification: Equation 7 changes the specified advantage normalization from normalization across trajectories at a fixed turn to pooling all turns across sampled trajectories, also reflected in Algorithm 1. This revises one calculation within the retained three-component GTPO design; it does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Section 6.2 adds GPQA Diamond, BBEH-mini, and EvalPlus HumanEval/MBPP evaluations, substantially extending coverage beyond mathematical reasoning to non-math reasoning and program synthesis. The five original math benchmarks and training datasets remain. Removing OlympiadBench from Table 2's caption corrects an unsupported listing rather than removing reported results.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 adds evaluated DAPO and SimpleTIR comparators on MATH 500 and AIME 2024 under the ablation training budget. This substantially broadens the trained-method comparison beyond GRPO. The original prompting and GRPO baselines remain; v1's conceptual DAPO comparison was not an empirical evaluation.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, EvalPlus testing, a three-embedding correlation protocol, and runtime-success rate as a tool-quality metric. These substantially broaden the evaluation design. Existing numerical training and evaluation settings in Section 5.1 and v1 Appendix A.2, retained as v2 A.4, remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Sections 6.3–6.4 add analyses testing whether code-similarity scores agree across embedding models and whether increased tool use accompanies executable code. These address robustness and tool errors beyond the original analyses. Existing component, discount, reward-shaping, and turn-count ablations remain, including the reward-shaping analysis relocated to Appendix A.5.

E5.justification: Section 6.3 newly introduces Pearson and Spearman correlation estimation for embedding-based similarity scores, reported in Table 8. Neither version reports training-seed replication, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the statistical addition does not quantify uncertainty in performance gains.

E6.justification: Original math scores and ablation values are retained, including v1 Tables 5–6 as v2 Tables 10–11. New Tables 5–9 add substantial results: Llama averages are 21.18 for GRPO versus 23.01 for GTPO, and non-math averages are 46.1 versus 47.9. Tool-execution success improves on average, but GTPO scores lower on AMC23: 69.49 versus GRPO's 72.17.

T1.justification: Equation 7 substantively revises the mathematical normalization set to include all trajectory-turn pairs. Section 4.3 also specifies the previously undefined no-positive-sample case. The turn-level MDP and discounted-return formulation remain, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from demonstrated mathematical-reasoning gains to non-math generalization, explicitly claiming 3.9% relative improvement on reasoning and program-synthesis tasks. They also foreground negligible overhead. The original three methodological contributions and 3.0% relative math-improvement claim remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting embedding-score correlations to reward-shaping robustness and execution success to reliable tool use. It explicitly acknowledges runtime success as a proxy that cannot establish logical correctness, and adds a qualitative overhead rationale. Table 4 also corrects gamma=1's interpretation from disabling turn-level rewards to disabling discounting.

D1.justification: v2 adds procedural pseudocode in Algorithm 1, documents global normalization and zero-positive handling, and identifies additional embedding models with access links. Appendix A.3 describes one embedding per trajectory and a rough seconds-level cost. Original hyperparameters and evaluation-setting disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: The redesigned Table 1 and new Appendix A.1 substantially expand positioning against GRPO/DAPO/GSPO and ReTool/ToRL/Search-R1, including an explicit first-formulation claim for the combined design. New benchmark and temporal-credit-assignment citations are added, while the SFT-related discussion and several associated references are removed.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the core narrative remain. v2 updates the title and affiliations, shortens parts of Related Work and Background, clarifies notation, adds a Discussion section and appendix explanations, and moves the reward-shaping discussion into the appendix. Rewriting of retained material is localized.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the conceptual comparison table and substantially expands experimental displays through Tables 5–9 and a full-width Algorithm 1. Several existing figures and tables are relocated, including the reward-shaping table becoming Appendix Table 10. All eight original figures retain their graphical content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the earlier paper's narrow empirical validation through matched DAPO/SimpleTIR comparisons, another model family, and four non-math benchmarks (Tables 5–7). The revised normalization specification and pseudocode also improve methodological clarity. These gains outweigh limitations in the additions: embedding correlations do not directly establish training robustness, overhead remains qualitatively argued, and Table 9's claim of consistent improvement contradicts its AMC23 result.
